I have been working this land for thirty years. I know what works. My husband and two sons do some work in the city now, so I need to manage the labor carefully. I cannot afford experiments. I will do what I have always done, adjusted for what worked last year and what the neighbors are doing.

My main income is the wheat-maize rotation on most of my land — around 8 mu. That land never rests idle. Wheat goes in after maize harvest in October, maize goes back in after wheat harvest in June. I keep 2.6 mu for cotton because the price is still decent and I know how to grow it, even though it is hard work and my back hurts more than it used to. The last 1 mu I put into mungbean — it is easy, the children can help, and we eat some ourselves.

For maize I will buy hybrid seed from the township supply shop, same brand as last year — 郑单958 or similar. For wheat I will use the improved variety the village cooperative sold last autumn. For cotton I will plant hybrid seed. Mungbean I saved my own seed.

I irrigate from the well. Wheat needs water before winter, at jointing, and at grain fill — three times. Maize I water at emergence if it is dry, at jointing, and at silking. Cotton I water more because the summer is dry and the bolls need moisture. Mungbean I water only if it looks stressed.

For fertilizer I use the compound bags plus urea on top for wheat and maize at jointing — I learned this rate from watching what gave the best ears in my plots. Cotton I fertilize heavier because it takes more from the soil. Mungbean barely needs nitrogen, it fixes its own.

Cotton spraying is the hardest part — bollworm can ruin the whole crop, so I spray six times through the season. Wheat I spray for aphids and rust in spring. Maize I spray herbicide right after planting and once more if stalk borer appears.

I rotary till before wheat planting and before cotton planting. For maize I just seed directly into the wheat stubble — saves time and moisture.
